transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because I just… I can’t stop noticing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw. It’s in every photo, every reflection, even in windows when I’m walking by—actually, the glass in office buildings is the worst, which is ridiculous because I work around buildings all day.

People keep telling me I look fine, but I don’t know how they don’t see it. It feels so obvious to me. And it’s gotten to where I’m avoiding presentations and meeting clients, which is a problem because that’s a big part of my work.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking your reflection throughout the day?

Yes. A lot. Before work especially, or if we’re going to some family thing, I can lose hours in the bathroom mirror. I’ll check one side, then the other, then take pictures on my phone from different angles because the mirror feels like it lies sometimes, but then the photos look worse.

And then I’ll redo my makeup, adjust my scarf, take it off, put it back on… my husband will be waiting by the door and I’ll ask him, “Does my face look lopsided today?” He always says no, but I don’t really believe him. Then sometimes I end up looking at other women’s photos online, comparing mine to theirs, which is not helpful, I know, but I still do it.
Do you feel like you have to perform these checking rituals or will you feel anxious if you don't?

Yes… I mean, I don’t think of it like a ritual exactly, but if I try not to check, I get really tense. Like before work, or if there’s a family event, I’ll tell myself I’m just going to look once and leave, but then I’m in the bathroom for ages—checking the mirror, taking phone pictures from different angles, redoing my makeup, changing my scarf.

And my husband will be waiting, and I’ll ask him again if my face looks lopsided, even though I already know what he’s going to say. Then sometimes I end up scrolling through photos of other women, comparing, which is stupid because it just makes me feel worse. But if I don’t do it, it’s like I can’t settle. I keep thinking, what if it really looks bad today and I didn’t catch it?
Is it only your face and jaw that you're concerned about, or are there other parts of your body that you worry about as well?

It’s mostly my face… the mouth and jaw area, that droop or unevenness. That’s the thing I can’t stop seeing. In photos, reflections, even like… walking past glass buildings, which I notice constantly because of work, and then I’m supposed to go into a meeting and act normal.

I know people say I look fine, but it feels so obvious to me. Like clients must be looking at it when I’m talking. So I’ve started avoiding presentations when I can, or trying to stay out of client meetings. I don’t really focus on other parts of my body the same way—it’s this part of my face that gets stuck in my head.
Do you think your face could ever look perfectly even and symmetrical to you, or do you believe it's inherently flawed in some way?

I don’t know… I think that’s the problem. Part of me keeps thinking if I just catch the right angle or fix my makeup the right way, maybe it’ll look even. But then every photo, every reflection, I see that droop around my mouth and jaw again.

It feels built in, like it’s just my face. And I know people say I look fine, but I can’t unsee it. I’ll be in a meeting, or even thinking about a presentation, and all I can imagine is clients staring at that uneven part while I’m talking. That’s why I’ve been avoiding presentations and clients when I can. It just feels too obvious.
Are you worried about other things being uneven or flawed besides your face?

Not really… I mean, I notice little things sometimes, like anyone does, but it doesn’t grab me the same way. It’s this droop around my mouth and my jaw, the unevenness there. I see it in every photo, every reflection, even when I’m just passing a window.

And then I’m supposed to go meet a client and talk about a design like I’m not thinking the whole time that they’re staring at it. I know people say I look fine, my husband says it, but it just feels so obvious to me. That’s why I’ve been avoiding presentations and client meetings when I can. It’s really that part of my face that I can’t stop seeing.
Has your concern about your face and jaw affected your relationships with friends and family, not just at work?

Yes… I mean, yes, it has. I try to tell myself it’s mainly work, but then it spills over. Like there was this awards thing—architectural awards, lots of people standing around with drinks and pretending not to judge each other’s shoes, you know—and I just couldn’t go. I kept thinking everyone would be looking at my face when I talked.

And family gatherings… I’ve started missing those or leaving things to the last minute until it all falls apart. My husband gets frustrated because we’ll have plans and then I can’t make myself get ready, or I’ll keep checking my face and suddenly we’re late or not going.

It’s embarrassing. I even cancelled a major client presentation at the last minute, which wasn’t family, I know, but it all feels connected. My deadlines are slipping, people are upset with me, and at home it’s like everything is revolving around whether I can stand being seen that day.
Do you think that even if someone proved to you that your face is symmetrical, you would still see it as uneven?

I think… yes, probably. I mean, even when people tell me it looks fine, or I try to convince myself a photo is just lighting, I still see that droop around my mouth and jaw. It’s like my eyes go straight to it.

And I know symmetry is one of those things architects talk about all the time—balance, proportion, all that—and maybe that makes me worse about it, I don’t know. But if someone showed me measurements or something, I think I’d still look in the mirror and feel like, no, it’s uneven. It just feels so obvious to me that I can’t stop checking for it, and then I don’t want clients or people in presentations looking at me.
Has your concern about your face and jaw started to affect your overall quality of life or daily activities outside of work?

Yes… it has. I keep thinking of it as “just” work, but it’s not. I mean, work is where it shows up in the biggest, most humiliating ways—like I cancelled a major client presentation at the last minute because I just couldn’t face being seen.

And then there are these award-related networking things I’m supposed to go to, and I know they matter. You see people, you make contacts, you pretend to enjoy tiny appetizers… but I’ve been missing those too. I’ll get dressed and then start looking at my face and suddenly I can’t go.

And it’s not staying neatly in one box. My project deadlines are slipping, and family gatherings are starting to fall apart because I either avoid them or make us late or just don’t go. It feels like everything gets planned around whether I can stand people looking at my face that day.
Do you ever find yourself having intrusive thoughts or compulsions to repeat certain behaviors that are not related to your appearance?

I’m not sure… not really, I don’t think. I mean, unless you count the checking, but that’s obviously about my face. Other than that, I don’t think I have rituals or anything.

I do get stuck on things sometimes, but I’ve always been particular—architecture sort of rewards that, you know, checking lines and details and whether something is level. My husband would probably say I fuss over things, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean. I haven’t noticed anything that feels separate from the face and jaw thing.
Are you feeling like your concerns about your face are affecting your relationship with your husband?

Yes… I mean, it’s hard to separate it out, because it feels like everything is affected lately. My husband sees me getting ready and then not leaving, or making us late because I’m stuck looking at my face, and then I get upset and he doesn’t know what to say.

It’s not just at home, though—like, I cancelled a major client presentation at the last minute because I couldn’t face being seen, and I’ve been missing those award networking events too. Those things sound work-related, but then I come home tense and ashamed, and it spills over. Project deadlines are slipping, family gatherings are falling apart… so yes, it’s definitely affecting us, even if I don’t always admit that to him.
Do you have any other thoughts or worries that you feel are excessive or uncontrollable, outside of your concerns about your face and jaw?

I don’t know… I’m trying to think. I mean, I worry about deadlines and whether clients are happy, but that feels like normal architect worry, if there is such a thing. Buildings have so many moving parts—permits, materials, people changing their minds after they’ve already approved something…

Sorry, that’s not really what you asked. Outside of my face and jaw, I don’t think there’s anything that feels that uncontrollable in the same way. I can get stressed, definitely, but I haven’t noticed some separate worry that takes over like this does.
Are there any areas of your life, besides your appearance, where you feel like you're excessively focused on details or flaws?

I’m not sure. I mean, in my work I notice flaws constantly—that’s part of the job, really. If a line is off or a material doesn’t sit right, it bothers me, but that feels… normal? Or at least normal for architects.

My husband jokes that I can spot a crooked picture frame from across a room, which is true, but I don’t think it takes over the way this does. Though now I’m thinking about this kitchen renovation we did years ago where the cabinet gaps were uneven and I kept pointing it out until everyone was sick of me—sorry, that’s probably not what you mean.

So… besides my appearance, I don’t know that there’s another area where it feels excessive in the same way.
Do you feel like your attention to detail at work is similar to how you focus on the details of your face?

Kind of, but it’s different. At work, if I’m looking at a drawing or a model, the details have a purpose. Like, a line being off actually changes something—sorry, I’m thinking of this facade detail that drove me crazy once because the shadow gap was wrong.

But with my face, it’s like I can’t let it go. I keep seeing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw, in every photo or reflection. Even when people say I look fine, it feels so obvious to me. And then I start thinking, how can I stand in front of clients like this? That’s when I avoid presentations or don’t want to meet people. So… no, it’s not really the same. It feels much more stuck.
Do you feel like your focus on the details of your face is similar to how you focus on details in other areas of your life?

It’s… similar in that I notice tiny things, I guess. Like if a line is off in a drawing, I’ll see it right away—actually there was this stair detail once that nobody else cared about and I couldn’t stop pointing at it, which probably drove everyone mad.

But my face feels different. That’s why I’m here, really. I can’t stop seeing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw, in every photo, every reflection. Even if someone says, “You look fine,” it doesn’t land. It feels so obvious to me that I start thinking everyone must be noticing it, and then I don’t want to give presentations or meet clients. So… yes and no. The attention to detail is familiar, but this is much more consuming.
Do you think you would be this bothered by small imperfections in other areas of your life if they weren't related to your appearance?

Not like this, no. I mean, I can get annoyed by things—like if a tile line is off, or a drawing has some tiny mistake, and then I’ll think about it longer than maybe I should. My husband would say I’m impossible about that sort of thing.

But… I’m here because of my face. Because I can’t stop seeing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw. It’s in every photo, every reflection, even a dark window sometimes—sorry, that sounds dramatic, but it’s true. And when people tell me I look fine, it doesn’t really help, because to me it feels so obvious.

With other imperfections, I might be irritated. With this, I start avoiding presentations and clients. So no, I don’t think other small flaws would bother me in the same way if they weren’t on me.
Do you find yourself being excessively critical of small imperfections in things other than your appearance, such as objects or tasks?

I’m not sure I’d call it excessive. I mean, I do notice things being off—especially in work things, like if a drawing isn’t lined up or a material sample looks wrong under the light. Architects are trained to notice that, you know? My first boss used to say if you miss a millimeter on paper it becomes a whole problem on site, which… I suppose stuck with me.

But outside of work? I don’t know. I can get fussy, maybe. Like if something in the house is crooked I’ll straighten it without thinking, or if a task isn’t done properly I might redo it. But I don’t know if that’s “excessively critical” or just… me being particular. My husband would probably have an opinion on that.
Do you think your tendency to notice and focus on small imperfections is something that applies to many areas of your life, not just your face?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, I do notice things, yes—probably more than some people. Like in a room, if something’s uneven, or in a plan if a line doesn’t quite meet, my eye goes there. But then again that’s also just… my job, isn’t it? You spend years being told to see those things.

Sorry, I’m wandering. With my face it feels different, but if you’re asking whether I’m like this everywhere in life… I don’t know. Maybe in some areas. I haven’t really thought about it that way. My husband would probably say yes before I would.
Do you think your attention to detail is something that helps you in your work as an architect, but becomes a problem when it comes to your own appearance?

Yes, I think that’s probably fair. I mean, at work it’s useful—if a line is off or a proportion doesn’t sit right, I can catch it before it becomes a bigger issue. That part of me has helped me, honestly.

But with my face it’s… it doesn’t feel useful. I’m here because I can’t stop seeing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw. It’s like my eye goes straight to it in every photo, every reflection—even when I’m just passing a shop window, which sounds ridiculous because I’m supposed to be thinking about errands or a client meeting, not my jaw.

And people say, “You look fine,” but I don’t feel fine. It feels so obvious to me that I’ve started avoiding presentations and clients, and that’s not like noticing a crooked detail in a drawing. That’s… that’s interfering with my life.

patient.answer:
Kind of, but it’s different. At work, if I’m looking at a drawing or a model, the details have a purpose. Like, a line being off actually changes something—sorry, I’m thinking of this facade detail that drove me crazy once because the shadow gap was wrong.

But with my face, it’s like I can’t let it go. I keep seeing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw, in every photo or reflection. Even when people say I look fine, it feels so obvious to me. And then I start thinking, how can I stand in front of clients like this? That’s when I avoid presentations or don’t want to meet people. So… no, it’s not really the same. It feels much more stuck.

doctor.question: Do you feel like your focus on the details of your face is similar to how you focus on details in other areas of your life?

patient.answer:
It’s… similar in that I notice tiny things, I guess. Like if a line is off in a drawing, I’ll see it right away—actually there was this stair detail once that nobody else cared about and I couldn’t stop pointing at it, which probably drove everyone mad.

But my face feels different. That’s why I’m here, really. I can’t stop seeing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw, in every photo, every reflection. Even if someone says, “You look fine,” it doesn’t land. It feels so obvious to me that I start thinking everyone must be noticing it, and then I don’t want to give presentations or meet clients. So… yes and no. The attention to detail is familiar, but this is much more consuming.

doctor.question: Do you think you would be this bothered by small imperfections in other areas of your life if they weren't related to your appearance?

target_item.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance

patient.answer:
Not like this, no. I mean, I can get annoyed by things—like if a tile line is off, or a drawing has some tiny mistake, and then I’ll think about it longer than maybe I should. My husband would say I’m impossible about that sort of thing.

But… I’m here because of my face. Because I can’t stop seeing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw. It’s in every photo, every reflection, even a dark window sometimes—sorry, that sounds dramatic, but it’s true. And when people tell me I look fine, it doesn’t really help, because to me it feels so obvious.

With other imperfections, I might be irritated. With this, I start avoiding presentations and clients. So no, I don’t think other small flaws would bother me in the same way if they weren’t on me.

doctor.question: Do you find yourself being excessively critical of small imperfections in things other than your appearance, such as objects or tasks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about being excessively critical of small imperfections in non-appearance-related objects or tasks, which is not covered by the listed Body Dysmorphic Disorder symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call it excessive. I mean, I do notice things being off—especially in work things, like if a drawing isn’t lined up or a material sample looks wrong under the light. Architects are trained to notice that, you know? My first boss used to say if you miss a millimeter on paper it becomes a whole problem on site, which… I suppose stuck with me.

But outside of work? I don’t know. I can get fussy, maybe. Like if something in the house is crooked I’ll straighten it without thinking, or if a task isn’t done properly I might redo it. But I don’t know if that’s “excessively critical” or just… me being particular. My husband would probably have an opinion on that.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure. I mean, I do notice things, yes—probably more than some people. Like in a room, if something’s uneven, or in a plan if a line doesn’t quite meet, my eye goes there. But then again that’s also just… my job, isn’t it? You spend years being told to see those things.

Sorry, I’m wandering. With my face it feels different, but if you’re asking whether I’m like this everywhere in life… I don’t know. Maybe in some areas. I haven’t really thought about it that way. My husband would probably say yes before I would.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think that’s probably fair. I mean, at work it’s useful—if a line is off or a proportion doesn’t sit right, I can catch it before it becomes a bigger issue. That part of me has helped me, honestly.

But with my face it’s… it doesn’t feel useful. I’m here because I can’t stop seeing this droop, this unevenness around my mouth and jaw. It’s like my eye goes straight to it in every photo, every reflection—even when I’m just passing a shop window, which sounds ridiculous because I’m supposed to be thinking about errands or a client meeting, not my jaw.

And people say, “You look fine,” but I don’t feel fine. It feels so obvious to me that I’ve started avoiding presentations and clients, and that’s not like noticing a crooked detail in a drawing. That’s… that’s interfering with my life.
